subject: Chemistry
question:
An acyclic alkene undergoes the following 5-step synthetic progression:
$$\text{3-methylpent-1-ene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Hg(OAc)_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ NaBH_4,\ OH^-}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_3PO_4}} \mathbf{C\ (major)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O_2,\ OH^-}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ B_2H_6 / THF}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ Collins\ reagent\ (CrO_3\cdot 2Py)}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Oxymercuration-demercuration of 3-methylpent-1-ene proceeds via Markovnikov hydration without carbocation rearrangement, yielding secondary alcohol B = 3-methylpentan-2-ol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
2. (iii) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H3PO4 protonates the -OH group. Departure of water generates a secondary carbocation at C2, which undergoes a rapid 1,2-hydride shift from C3 to form the more stable tertiary carbocation CH3-CH2-C+(CH3)-CH2CH3. Subsequent elimination of a proton gives the most substituted, symmetrical alkene: C = 3-methylpent-2-ene.
3. (iv) Hydroboration-oxidation adds B2H6 anti-Markovnikov (syn addition) across the trisubstituted alkene to place the hydroxyl group at C2, regenerating secondary alcohol D = 3-methylpentan-2-ol.
4. (v) Collins reagent (CrO3.2Py in CH2Cl2) cleanly oxidizes the secondary alcohol to ketone E = 3-methylpentan-2-one.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Cascade linking non-rearranged Markovnikov hydration, hydride-shift dehydration, hydroboration regiocontrol, and mild Collins oxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: OMDM -> 1,2-hydride shift dehydration -> Hydroboration-oxidation -> Collins oxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Oxymercuration-demercuration, tertiary carbocation hydride shift, Zaitsev alkene, hydroboration, chromium oxidation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Integrates OMDM with Wagner-Meerwein hydride rearrangement and subsequent selective hydroboration-oxidation.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Consider the series of phenolic and benzylic functional group conversions:
$$\text{p-Cresol (4-methylphenol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)\ excess\ Br_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_3I,\ K_2CO_3}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{\Delta}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ alkaline\ KMnO_4;\ then\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ SOCl_2}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{BaSO_4,\ quinoline}]{\mathrm{(v)\ H_2,\ Pd}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Bromination of 4-methylphenol with excess bromine in water: Because the para position is blocked by the methyl group, electrophilic bromination occurs exclusively and completely at both vacant ortho positions relative to the activating -OH group, yielding A = 2,6-dibromo-4-methylphenol.
2. (ii) Williamson ether synthesis with CH3I and K2CO3 converts the phenolic hydroxyl into an ether, yielding B = 1,3-dibromo-2-methoxy-5-methylbenzene.
3. (iii) Vigorous oxidation of the benzylic methyl group with hot alkaline KMnO4 followed by acidification converts the methyl group into a carboxylic acid, giving C = 3,5-dibromo-4-methoxybenzoic acid.
4. (iv) Reaction with thionyl chloride (SOCl2) converts the carboxylic acid to acyl chloride D = 3,5-dibromo-4-methoxybenzoyl chloride.
5. (v) Rosenmund reduction (H2/Pd-BaSO4 poisoned with quinoline) selectively reduces the acid chloride to aldehyde E = 3,5-dibromo-4-methoxybenzaldehyde without reducing the methoxy or bromo substituents.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Phenolic ortho-polybromination coupled with etherification, benzylic permanganate oxidation, and Rosenmund reduction.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Aqueous bromination -> Williamson methylation -> Benzylic oxidation -> Acyl chloride formation -> Rosenmund reduction.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Phenol activating directing effects, ether protection, benzylic oxidation, Rosenmund catalytic reduction.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Combines phenol functionalization with side-chain oxidation and poisoned catalytic reduction to an aldehyde.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A cyclic monoterpene derivative undergoes the following sequence:
$$\text{Cyclohex-2-en-1-one} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CH_3MgBr\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(ii)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{B\ (conjugated)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ 1\ eq.\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ LiAlH_4,\ then\ H_2O}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ Dess-Martin\ periodinane}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major structural product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) 1,2-addition of methylmagnesium bromide (CH3MgBr) to the carbonyl of cyclohex-2-en-1-one followed by protonation gives tertiary allylic alcohol A = 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
2. (ii) Acid-catalyzed dehydration of A with hot H2SO4 yields conjugated diene B = 1-methylcyclohexa-1,3-diene.
3. (iii) Selective mono-epoxidation with 1 equivalent mCPBA occurs preferentially at the more electron-rich, more substituted alkene double bond (C1=C2) to form mono-epoxide C.
4. (iv) Regioselective hydride reduction of C with LiAlH4 attacks the epoxide at the less substituted carbon, leaving allylic alcohol D = 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
5. (v) Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP) oxidizes the secondary allylic alcohol cleanly to conjugated enone E = 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Cyclic enone Grignard addition followed by diene generation, chemoselective epoxidation, hydride opening, and periodinane oxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: 1,2-Grignard addition -> Dehydration -> Chemoselective epoxidation -> LiAlH4 opening -> DMP oxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Enone 1,2-addition, conjugated diene synthesis, peracid diene chemoselectivity, allylic alcohol oxidation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Controls regiochemistry across a conjugated cyclic diene to synthesize 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.

subject: Chemistry
question:
The following reaction pathway exploits selective ether opening and functionalization:
$$\text{Propylene oxide (2-methyloxirane)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)\ dil.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ TsCl\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{B\ (selective)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ NaCN,\ DMSO}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Acid-catalyzed hydration of propylene oxide opens the oxirane ring to give propane-1,2-diol (A).
2. (ii) Selective monotosylation with 1 eq. TsCl in pyridine esterifies the sterically unhindered primary alcohol preferentially over the secondary alcohol, giving B = 2-hydroxypropyl 4-methylbenzenesulfonate.
3. (iii) SN2 displacement of the primary tosylate with NaCN in DMSO produces C = 3-hydroxybutanenitrile (or 4-hydroxypentanenitrile upon chain extension).
4. (iv) Acidic hydrolysis converts the nitrile to a carboxylic acid, yielding gamma-hydroxy acid D = 4-hydroxypentanoic acid.
5. (v) Intramolecular Fischer esterification (lactonization): Heating in the presence of catalytic H2SO4 drives spontaneous cyclization with loss of water, forming the thermodynamically favored 5-membered cyclic ester (gamma-lactone): E = 5-methyldihydrofuran-2(3H)-one (gamma-valerolactone).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Oxirane hydration followed by primary-selective monotosylation, cyanide substitution, nitrile hydrolysis, and gamma-lactonization.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Acidic oxirane opening -> Primary-selective tosylation -> Cyanation -> Acid hydrolysis -> Intramolecular lactonization.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Steric discrimination in diol tosylation, cyanide SN2 displacement, nitrile hydrolysis, gamma-lactone formation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Exploits steric differentiation between 1° and 2° alcohols to direct sequential nitrile homologation and lactonization.

subject: Chemistry
question:
An aromatic ether undergoes rearrangement and tandem transformations:
$$\text{Guaiacol (2-methoxyphenol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{acetone}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Allyl\ bromide,\ K_2CO_3}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{215^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ (CH_3CO)_2O,\ pyridine}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ O_3;\ then\ Zn / AcOH}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ 1\ eq.\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ formed via the Claisen rearrangement is:
explanation:
1. (i) Allylation of guaiacol (2-methoxyphenol) with allyl bromide in K2CO3/acetone yields allyl 2-methoxyphenyl ether (A).
2. Heating to 215°C induces an aromatic [3,3]-sigmatropic Claisen rearrangement. In guaiacol, position 1 is -OH and position 2 is -OCH3. The allyl group migrates preferentially to the vacant ortho position (position 6) to give 6-allyl-2-methoxyphenol (B).
3. Migration to the para position (yielding 4-allyl-2-methoxyphenol / eugenol) only occurs when BOTH ortho positions are blocked; since position 6 is unhindered and open, the ortho Claisen product 6-allyl-2-methoxyphenol forms exclusively.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Aromatic Claisen rearrangement in unsymmetrically substituted ortho-methoxyphenols.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Aromatic [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement -> Ortho-site regiochemical preference.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Aromatic Claisen rearrangement, ortho vs para migration preferences, guaiacol ether chemistry.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Enforces strict mechanistic distinction: ortho migration predominates whenever an ortho position is unoccupied.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A symmetrical vicinal diol cascade is carried out as follows:
$$\text{cis-Cyclohexane-1,2-diol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ excess\ DMP}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ excess\ CH_3MgBr}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ HIO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ NaBH_4,\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{E}$$
The terminal product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) DMP oxidation of cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol oxidizes both secondary alcohol groups cleanly to a 1,2-dicarbonyl: cyclohexane-1,2-dione (A).
2. (ii) Addition of excess methylmagnesium bromide followed by aqueous quench adds two methyl groups to form di-tertiary diol B = 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane-1,2-diol.
3. (iii) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H2SO4 yields 1,2-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene or octanedione precursor C.
4. (iv) Cleavage with periodic acid/oxidant yields dicarbonyl D = octane-2,7-dione.
5. (v) Reduction with NaBH4 reduces the two carbonyl groups to secondary alcohols, delivering terminal product E = octane-2,7-diol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Vicinal diol bis-oxidation followed by dual Grignard addition, dehydration, cleavage, and borohydride reduction.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: DMP bis-oxidation -> Dual Grignard addition -> Dehydration -> C-C cleavage -> NaBH4 reduction.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: 1,2-dione synthesis, organometallic additions to alpha-diones, periodic cleavage, secondary diol reduction.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Connects cyclic 1,2-diol oxidation with dialkyl Grignard substitution and acyclic diol reconstruction.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Evaluate the following cascade involving an unsymmetrical epoxide:
$$\text{Phenyloxirane (Styrene oxide)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3OH}]{\mathrm{(i)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ SOCl_2,\ pyridine}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ alc.\ KOH}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Br_2}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ NaNH_2,\ liquid\ NH_3}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Acid-catalyzed methanolysis of styrene oxide: Protonation of the epoxide is followed by nucleophilic attack of methanol at the benzylic carbon (C2) where positive charge is resonance-stabilized by the phenyl ring, yielding A = 2-methoxy-2-phenylethan-1-ol.
2. (ii) Chlorination of the primary alcohol with SOCl2 in pyridine gives B = 2-chloro-1-methoxy-1-phenylethane.
3. (iii) Base-promoted dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH eliminates HCl to form the conjugated enol ether: C = (2-methoxyvinyl)benzene, Ph-CH=CH-OCH3.
4. (iv) Addition of Br2 across the enol ether double bond forms dibromide D = 1,2-dibromo-2-methoxy-1-phenylethane.
5. (v) Treatment with excess strong base NaNH2 in liquid NH3 triggers tandem E2 eliminations (expelling two moles of HBr and one mole of methanol / methoxide), generating terminal alkyne E = phenylacetylene (ethynylbenzene).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Acid-catalyzed epoxide methanolysis followed by chlorination, enol ether formation, bromination, and sodamide double elimination.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Benzylic epoxide methanolysis -> SOCl2 chlorination -> E2 to enol ether -> Bromination -> Double elimination to alkyne.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Styrene oxide regioselective opening, enol ether synthesis, vicinal dihalide elimination, terminal alkyne formation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates synthesis of phenylacetylene through an enol ether bromination-elimination cascade.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Consider the series of electrophilic substitutions and cleavage steps on phenol:
$$\text{Phenol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{con.\ H_2SO_4,\ 373\text{ K}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ con.\ HNO_3}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ PCl_5}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ Benzene}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Sn\ (excess)}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{273-278\text{ K}}]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ NaNO_2,\ HCl;\ then\ H_3PO_2}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Vigorous nitration of phenol with concentrated HNO3/H2SO4 at 373 K yields picric acid, A = 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
2. (ii) Reaction of picric acid with PCl5 displaces the phenolic -OH group with chlorine to form picryl chloride, B = 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene.
3. (iii) Friedel-Crafts arylation of benzene with picryl chloride in AlCl3 displaces the activated chlorine to produce 2,4,6-trinitrobiphenyl (C).
4. (iv) Exhaustive reduction of the three nitro groups with Sn/HCl produces biphenyl-2,4,6-triamine (D).
5. (v) Diazotization with excess NaNO2/HCl followed by hypophosphorous acid (H3PO2) deamination removes the three amino groups, or under coupling gives polyphenyls; here meta-substituted terphenyl array delivers E = 1,1':3',1''-terphenyl.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Phenol picric acid functionalization cascaded with Friedel-Crafts arylation, poly-reduction, and deaminative manipulation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Vigorous nitration -> Chlorination -> Friedel-Crafts arylation -> Poly-nitro reduction -> Diazotization deamination.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Picric acid, picryl chloride activation, Friedel-Crafts arylation, poly-diazotization, hypophosphorous acid deamination.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Manipulates trinitrophenol through ipso-chlorination, arylation, and deaminative skeleton construction.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A primary aliphatic alcohol is traced through the sequence:
$$\text{Neopentyl alcohol (2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol)} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(i)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ B_2H_6 / THF;\ then\ H_2O_2,\ OH^-}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ PDC}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ C_2H_5MgBr}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ Cu\ at\ 573\text{ K}}} \mathbf{E}$$
The structural formula of ketone $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Dehydration of neopentyl alcohol, (CH3)3C-CH2OH: Protonation and departure of water is accompanied by a 1,2-methyl shift to avoid an unstable primary carbocation, yielding tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C(+)-CH2CH3. Elimination gives A = 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3.
2. (ii) Hydroboration-oxidation adds H and OH anti-Markovnikov to the less substituted carbon, giving secondary alcohol B = 3-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH3)2CH-CH(OH)CH3.
3. (iii) Oxidation with PDC gives ketone C = 3-methylbutan-2-one, (CH3)2CH-CO-CH3.
4. (iv) Addition of ethylmagnesium bromide (C2H5MgBr) adds an ethyl group, yielding tertiary/secondary alcohol intermediates; oxidation over Cu at 573 K delivers ketone E = 4-methylhexan-3-one.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Neopentyl carbocation rearrangement dehydration coupled with hydroboration, PDC oxidation, Grignard addition, and catalytic Cu oxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Wagner-Meerwein methyl shift -> Hydroboration -> PDC oxidation -> Grignard addition -> Cu/573 K oxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Neopentyl alcohol rearrangement, hydroboration regiocontrol, Grignard carbonyl additions, catalytic copper reactions.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Rigorous treatment of neopentyl skeletal rearrangement combined with regiospecific functionalization.

subject: Chemistry
question:
The following reaction pathway investigates the abnormal Reimer--Tiemann reaction:
$$\text{Indole} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{100^\circ C}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CHCl_3,\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{A\ (ring-expanded)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ H_2,\ Pt}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ CH_3I}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ moist\ Ag_2O}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ pyrolysis}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major heterocyclic skeleton in intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Abnormal Reimer-Tiemann reaction: In the presence of aqueous base and chloroform, dichlorocarbene (:CCl2) is generated.
2. Attack of dichlorocarbene on the C2=C3 double bond of indole forms a dichlorocyclopropane intermediate fused to the pyrrole ring.
3. Spontaneous ring expansion with loss of chloride ion (driven by rearomatization) expands the 5-membered pyrrole ring into a 6-membered pyridine ring, delivering A = 3-chloroquinoline.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Abnormal Reimer-Tiemann dichlorocarbene insertion and ring expansion of indole.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Carbene cycloaddition -> Dichlorocyclopropane intermediate -> Ring-expansion dehalogenation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Dichlorocarbene reactivity, abnormal Reimer-Tiemann reaction, indole ring expansion, quinoline synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Unambiguously demonstrates the abnormal Reimer-Tiemann ring expansion to 3-chloroquinoline.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A spirocyclic ether is constructed via the cascade:
$$\text{Cyclopentyl bromide} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ ether}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Mg}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Cyclobutanone}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{C\ (rearranged)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(v)\ LiAlH_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Alcohol $\mathbf{B}$ undergoes ring expansion upon treatment with $\ce{con. H2SO4}$ in step (iii). Alkene $\mathbf{C}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Cyclopentylmagnesium bromide adds to cyclobutanone followed by protonation to form tertiary alcohol B = 1-cyclopentylcyclobutan-1-ol.
2. (iii) Protonation of the tertiary alcohol followed by loss of water generates a cyclobutyl carbocation with adjacent cyclopentyl ring. To relieve high four-membered ring strain, a 1,2-bond shift expands the 4-membered ring to a 5-membered ring. Elimination of a proton yields the highly symmetrical, strain-relieved alkene: C = bicyclopentylidene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Grignard cycloalkanone addition followed by strain-relieved carbocation ring expansion to bicyclopentylidene.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Grignard addition -> Acid-catalyzed ring expansion -> Alkene elimination.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Cyclobutanone reactivity, strain relief in carbocation rearrangements, ring expansion, symmetric alkene synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Highlights dramatic strain relief in converting 1-cyclopentylcyclobutan-1-ol into bicyclopentylidene.

subject: Chemistry
question:
The behavior of hindered aromatic ethers with Lewis acids is evaluated below:
$$\text{2,6-di-tert-butylphenol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMF}]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaH,\ then\ CH_3I}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ BBr_3\ (1\ eq.,\ -78^\circ\text{C});\ then\ H_2O}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ CH_2O,\ (CH_3)_2NH}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ CH_3I}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{A}$ fails to form in significant yield if step (i) uses:
explanation:
1. Potassium 2,6-di-tert-butylphenolate is an extremely sterically hindered, bulky phenoxide base.
2. When reacted with a tertiary alkyl halide such as tert-butyl bromide, (CH3)3C-Br, SN2 nucleophilic substitution is completely blocked by steric hindrance.
3. The phenoxide acts exclusively as a Brønsted base, inducing rapid E2 elimination of tert-butyl bromide to form 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) and regenerating the phenol. No Williamson ether substitution occurs.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Steric constraints in Williamson ether synthesis comparing methylating agents against tertiary alkyl halides.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Steric hindrance evaluation -> Base vs nucleophile competition -> E2 pathway dominance.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Hindered phenoxides, Williamson ether synthesis limitations, SN2 vs E2 competition.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Pinpoints exclusive E2 elimination when bulky phenoxides encounter tertiary alkyl halides.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Trace the products in the following multi-step transformation:
$$\text{Cyclohexene} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(i)\ NBS,\ CCl_4,\ h\nu}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O_2,\ OH^-}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ (1)\ mCPBA\ (syn\ directed)}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ NaBH_4,\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ HIO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
If step (iii) produces cis-2,3-epoxycyclohexan-1-ol ($\mathbf{C}$) and step (iv) selectively opens the epoxide to yield a cyclohexane-1,3-diol ($\mathbf{D}$), product $\mathbf{E}$ upon treatment with $\ce{HIO4}$ will:
options: Not react, because HIO4 is specific for vicinal diols
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Allylic bromination of cyclohexene followed by hydrolysis gives allylic alcohol B = cyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
2. (iii) mCPBA directed by the allylic -OH gives cis-2,3-epoxycyclohexan-1-ol (C).
3. (iv) Reduction opens the epoxide ring to produce cyclohexane-1,3-diol (D).
4. (v) Periodic acid (HIO4, Malaprade reagent) specifically cleaves only 1,2-diols (vicinal diols) via a cyclic 5-membered periodate diester intermediate. Because compound D is a 1,3-diol, it cannot form this cyclic intermediate and is completely unreactive toward HIO4.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Allylic functionalization to 1,3-diol and probe of periodate reagent structural specificity.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Allylic bromination -> Hydrolysis -> Directed epoxidation -> 1,3-diol opening -> Periodate specificity test.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Allylic functionalization, directed epoxidation, Malaprade reaction mechanism, 1,2- vs 1,3-diol discrimination.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Tests crucial mechanistic requirement: HIO4 requires a cyclic periodate ester achievable ONLY with vicinal diols.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Determine the final target $\mathbf{E}$ in the sequence:
$$\text{Phenol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{(i)\ (CH_3)_2CHCH_2Cl}} \mathbf{A\ (major)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ TsCl}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ Br_2,\ Fe}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ aq.\ NaOH\ (reflux)}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ con.\ HNO_3,\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Friedel-Crafts alkylation of phenol with isobutyl chloride, (CH3)2CHCH2Cl, in the presence of AlCl3:
2. The nascent primary isobutyl cation immediately undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form the far more stable tertiary carbocation: the tert-butyl cation, (CH3)3C+.
3. Electrophilic attack by the bulky tert-butyl cation on the strongly activated phenoxy ring occurs with overwhelming selectivity at the less hindered para position, yielding A = 4-tert-butylphenol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Friedel-Crafts alkylation of phenol with isobutyl halide exhibiting spontaneous carbocation rearrangement.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Primary to tertiary hydride shift -> Steric-controlled para-EAS substitution.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Friedel-Crafts alkylation, carbocation rearrangement, steric control in phenol EAS.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Reinforces classic rearrangement converting isobutyl halides into tert-butylated phenols.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A stereochemical relay of reactions is initiated on cyclohexene:
$$\text{Cyclohexene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Br_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMSO}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ excess\ NaOCH_3,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ mCPBA\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3OH}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ PCC}} \mathbf{E}$$
Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Anti-addition of bromine across cyclohexene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (A).
2. (ii) Heating trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane with excess sodium methoxide (a strong base) in DMSO triggers two consecutive E2 eliminations.
3. The second elimination is thermodynamically driven to form the resonance-stabilized conjugated diene, cyclohexa-1,3-diene (B), rather than the unconjugated 1,4-diene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Halogenation of cycloalkene followed by thermodynamic double dehydrohalogenation to conjugated diene.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Anti-bromination -> Tandem E2 eliminations -> Conjugated diene formation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Alkene bromination, E2 elimination, conjugated vs non-conjugated diene stability.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Highlights thermodynamic driving force favoring conjugated cyclohexa-1,3-diene over cyclohexa-1,4-diene.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Consider the behavior of tertiary alcohols in the Victor Meyer test sequence:
$$\text{2-Methylpropan-2-ol} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(i)\ P + I_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ AgNO_2}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ HNO_2\ (NaNO_2 + HCl)}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Which observation correctly describes intermediate $\mathbf{C}$ and solution $\mathbf{D}$?
options: C forms a red nitrolic acid salt with NaOH (D is blood-red).
C forms a blue pseudonitrol (D is deep blue).
B does not react with HNO2; hence C and D remain completely colorless.
B hydrolyzes to give an alkene that oxidizes to an intensely yellow dinitro compound.
explanation:
1. (i) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol) reacts with P + I2 to form 2-iodo-2-methylpropane (A).
2. (ii) Nucleophilic substitution with AgNO2 yields 2-methyl-2-nitropropane, (CH3)3C-NO2 (B).
3. (iii) Because the alpha-carbon bearing the nitro group has NO hydrogen atoms (tertiary nitroalkane), it cannot undergo reaction with nitrous acid (HNO2). Thus, intermediate C does not form.
4. (iv) Addition of aqueous NaOH produces no color change; the solution remains completely colorless (distinguishing tertiary alcohols from 1° red nitrolic acid and 2° blue pseudonitrol).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Qualitative Victor Meyer alcohol distinction evaluated through tertiary nitroalkane inertness.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Victor Meyer test sequence -> Lack of alpha-hydrogens -> Negative color response.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Victor Meyer test, 1°/2°/3° alcohol distinction, nitroalkane tautomerism, nitrolic acid vs pseudonitrol.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Unpacks the exact mechanistic rationale for why 3° alcohols yield a colorless result in Victor Meyer's test.

subject: Chemistry
question:
In the following synthesis starting from an ether:
$$\text{Anisole} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{(i)\ (CH_3CO)_2O}} \mathbf{A\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ I_2,\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{B} + \ce{CHI3}\downarrow \quad \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ excess\ con.\ HI,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ Br_2,\ H_2O}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole with acetic anhydride gives 4-methoxyacetophenone (A).
2. (ii)-(iii) Haloform reaction with I2/NaOH followed by acidification oxidizes the methyl ketone to carboxylic acid C = 4-methoxybenzoic acid (p-anisic acid) with precipitation of iodoform (CHI3).
3. (iv) Demethylation with excess hot concentrated HI cleaves the aryl methyl ether to deliver D = 4-hydroxybenzoic acid.
4. (v) Bromination of 4-hydroxybenzoic acid with excess bromine water: The strongly activating phenolic -OH group activates positions 2, 4, and 6. Electrophilic attack occurs at both open ortho positions (2 and 6) and triggers ipso-bromination at position 4 with simultaneous decarboxylation (-CO2), delivering E = 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Anisole acylation followed by haloform degradation, ether cleavage, and ipso-decarboxylative bromination.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Friedel-Crafts acylation -> Haloform reaction -> HI ether cleavage -> Ipso-bromination decarboxylation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Aromatic acylation, haloform reaction, aryl ether cleavage, phenolic ipso-substitution decarboxylation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Tests facile ipso-bromination with decarboxylative loss of -COOH in activated 4-hydroxybenzoic acid.

subject: Chemistry
question:
An allylic alcohol cascade proceeds via:
$$\text{Allyl alcohol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ PBr_3}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{THF}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Sodium\ phenolate}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{200^\circ C}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ con.\ HBr\ (excess),\ \Delta}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMF}]{\mathrm{(v)\ NaH}} \mathbf{E}$$
The terminal product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) PBr3 converts allyl alcohol into allyl bromide (A).
2. (ii) Williamson ether synthesis with sodium phenolate gives allyl phenyl ether (B).
3. (iii) Heating to 200°C induces [3,3]-sigmatropic Claisen rearrangement to form 2-allylphenol (C).
4. (iv) Markovnikov addition of concentrated HBr across the terminal alkene yields secondary bromide D = 2-(2-bromopropyl)phenol.
5. (v) Treatment with NaH deprotonates the phenol to phenoxide, which undergoes intramolecular SN2 displacement of bromide, closing a 5-membered cyclic ether: E = 2-methyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Allylic bromination cascaded into Williamson etherification, Claisen rearrangement, and intramolecular cyclization.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: PBr3 halogenation -> Williamson synthesis -> Claisen rearrangement -> Markovnikov hydrobromination -> 5-exo-tet cyclization.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Allylic conversion, Claisen rearrangement, Markovnikov addition, dihydrobenzofuran synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Unifies primary allylic functionalization with sigmatropic rearrangement and intramolecular etherification.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Trace the intermediates in the ring-expansion cascade:
$$\text{Cyclobutanol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ PCC}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_3MgBr}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O_2,\ OH^-}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ B_2H_6 / THF}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ DMP}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{C}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) PCC oxidizes cyclobutanol to cyclobutanone (A).
2. (ii) Methylmagnesium bromide addition followed by hydrolysis yields tertiary alcohol B = 1-methylcyclobutan-1-ol.
3. (iii) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H2SO4: Elimination of water from the tertiary alcohol occurs with Zaitsev regioselectivity to form the endocyclic, more substituted alkene: C = 1-methylcyclobut-1-ene (more stable than exocyclic methylenecyclobutane).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Cyclobutanol oxidation followed by Grignard addition and regioselective endocyclic dehydration.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: PCC oxidation -> Grignard addition -> Zaitsev endocyclic dehydration.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Four-membered ring chemistry, Grignard additions to cyclobutanone, endocyclic vs exocyclic alkene stability.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Reinforces formation of the more substituted endocyclic double bond in 1-methylcyclobut-1-ene.

subject: Chemistry
subTopic: Aryl Alkyl Ether Cleavage with HI
question:
An aryl bromide undergoes organometallic addition to an epoxide:
$$\text{Bromobenzene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ ether}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Mg}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Oxirane\ (ethylene\ oxide)}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ TsCl}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ Sodium\ phenolate,\ DMF}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ 1\ equivalent\ con.\ HI\ (cold)}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic products obtained from the ether cleavage in step (v) are:
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Phenylmagnesium bromide adds to ethylene oxide to give 2-phenylethan-1-ol (B).
2. (iii)-(iv) Tosylation of B followed by reaction with sodium phenolate produces aryl alkyl ether D = (2-phenoxyethyl)benzene, Ph-O-CH2CH2Ph.
3. (v) Ether cleavage with 1 equivalent cold HI: Protonation gives Ph-O+(H)-CH2CH2Ph. The aromatic C-O bond possesses partial double-bond character due to resonance and cannot be attacked via SN2. Iodide selectively attacks the primary aliphatic carbon via an SN2 displacement, releasing Phenol and (2-iodoethyl)benzene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Grignard oxirane homologation to aryl alkyl ether followed by mechanistically rigorous cold HI cleavage.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Grignard epoxide opening -> Tosylation -> Williamson synthesis -> Regioselective HI ether cleavage.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Oxirane C2-homologation, Williamson ether synthesis, differential cleavage of aryl alkyl ethers with HI.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Highlights resonance-inertness of sp2 aryl-oxygen bond during hydroiodic acid ether cleavage.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Pinacolone undergoes the following transformation sequence:
$$\text{Pinacolone (3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(i)\ NaBH_4,\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(ii)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{B\ (major)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ CF_3CO_3H}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3OH}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ PCC}} \mathbf{E}$$
Alkene $\mathbf{B}$ formed via 1,2-methyl shift is:
explanation:
1. (i) NaBH4 reduction of pinacolone gives secondary alcohol A = 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
2. (ii) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H2SO4: Protonation and departure of water generates secondary carbocation (CH3)3C-CH(+)-CH3.
3. A rapid 1,2-methyl shift forms the more stable tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C(+)-CH(CH3)2.
4. Elimination of a proton follows the Zaitsev rule to form the tetrasubstituted, thermodynamically most stable alkene: B = 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Pinacolone reduction followed by acid-catalyzed dehydration driven by Wagner-Meerwein 1,2-methyl shift.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Borohydride reduction -> Wagner-Meerwein methyl shift -> Zaitsev elimination.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Ketone reduction, secondary to tertiary carbocation rearrangement, tetrasubstituted alkene stability.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Standardizes the classic Wagner-Meerwein methyl shift occurring upon dehydration of 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A bicyclic ether system is probed through the sequence:
$$\text{trans-2-Bromocyclohexan-1-ol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{THF}]{\mathrm{(i)\ t-BuOK}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_3CH_2MgBr}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_3PO_4}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ O_3;\ then\ (CH_3)_2S}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ NaBH_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ and product $\mathbf{B}$ are, respectively:
explanation:
1. (i) Treatment of trans-2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol with potassium tert-butoxide causes deprotonation of -OH; the resulting alkoxide performs an intramolecular SN2 attack with backside displacement of bromide, closing the oxirane ring: A = cyclohexene oxide (7-oxabicyclo[4.1.0]heptane).
2. (ii) Nucleophilic addition of ethylmagnesium bromide to symmetrical epoxide A proceeds via backside SN2 attack with inversion, yielding B = trans-2-ethylcyclohexan-1-ol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Intramolecular halohydrin cyclization to oxirane followed by stereospecific Grignard ring opening.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Intramolecular SN2 cyclization -> Grignard epoxide opening with inversion.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Halohydrin to epoxide conversion, stereospecific SN2 oxirane opening by Grignard reagents.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates trans-stereospecificity in both oxirane closure and subsequent Grignard opening.

subject: Chemistry
question:
The Fries rearrangement of aryl esters is extended below:
$$\text{p-Cresol (4-methylphenol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Benzoyl\ chloride\ (C_6H_5COCl)}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(ii)\ anhydrous\ AlCl_3}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ Br_2,\ FeBr_3}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ (1)\ NaBH_4;\ (2)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Esterification of 4-methylphenol with benzoyl chloride in pyridine gives 4-methylphenyl benzoate (A).
2. (ii) Fries rearrangement with anhydrous AlCl3: Thermal rearrangement migrates the benzoyl group to an open position activated by the phenolic oxygen. Since the para position is occupied by the methyl group, migration occurs exclusively to the vacant ortho position, yielding B = (2-hydroxy-5-methylphenyl)(phenyl)methanone.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Phenolic benzoylation followed by regioselective ortho-Fries rearrangement.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Aryl ester synthesis -> Ortho-selective Fries rearrangement.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Aryl esters, Fries rearrangement directing factors, para-blocked phenolics.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Illustrates exclusive ortho-Fries rearrangement when the para position is blocked by an alkyl group.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Crown ether catalyzed substitution followed by ether cleavage:
$$\text{Benzyl chloride} \xrightarrow[\text{18-crown-6,\ benzene}]{\mathrm{(i)\ KF}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{h\nu}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ NBS\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ Sodium\ ethoxide,\ ethanol}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ excess\ con.\ HBr,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{ether}]{\mathrm{(v)\ Mg;\ then\ CO_2;\ then\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{E}$$
The role of 18-crown-6 in step (i) is to:
options: Solvate the fluoride ion, making it a stronger electrophile
Specifically complex the potassium cation (K+), exposing 'naked' and highly nucleophilic F-
Act as a phase-transfer acid catalyst
Invert the stereochemistry at the benzylic center
explanation:
1. Potassium fluoride (KF) is an ionic salt insoluble in non-polar organic solvents like benzene.
2. The macrocyclic cavity of 18-crown-6 (diameter ~2.6-3.2 Å) selectively coordinates and encapsulates potassium cations (K+, ionic diameter 2.66 Å).
3. By sequestering K+ into the organic phase, the fluoride counteranion (F-) is pulled into benzene without a solvent shell ('naked fluoride'). Unsolvated fluoride is exceptionally nucleophilic and readily displaces benzylic chloride to form benzyl fluoride (A).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Crown ether host-guest supramolecular complexation evaluated for nucleophilic activation of insoluble salts.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Host-guest cation sequestration -> Anion naked activation -> Nucleophilic fluorination.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Crown ethers, cavity size complementarity, naked fluoride nucleophilicity, phase transfer.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Explains supramolecular basis of 18-crown-6 activation of insoluble KF in non-polar solvents.

subject: Chemistry
question:
The final 5-step cascade features cyclic ethers and migratory aptitude:
$$\text{Benzophenone (diphenylmethanone)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMSO}]{\mathrm{(i)\ (CH_3)_3S^+I^-\ (Corey-Chaykovsky)}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ BF_3\cdot OEt_2}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ PhMgBr}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ O_3;\ then\ Me_2S}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ formed via ring expansion/rearrangement of epoxide $\mathbf{A}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Corey-Chaykovsky epoxidation: Dimethylsulfonium methylide transfers a methylene group (:CH2) to benzophenone to produce 2,2-diphenyloxirane (A).
2. (ii) Lewis acid catalyzed rearrangement: Coordination of BF3.OEt2 to the epoxide oxygen triggers oxirane opening to form a tertiary benzylic carbocation Ph2C(+)-CH2-O-BF3(-).
3. A rapid 1,2-hydride shift from the adjacent methylene carbon followed by regeneration of the carbonyl produces diphenylacetaldehyde, B = Ph2CH-CHO.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Corey-Chaykovsky sulfur ylide epoxidation followed by Lewis-acid catalyzed 1,2-hydride shift rearrangement.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Corey-Chaykovsky reaction -> BF3-promoted epoxide opening -> 1,2-hydride shift to aldehyde.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Sulfur ylides, oxirane synthesis, Lewis acid catalyzed epoxide rearrangements, migratory aptitude.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Traces Corey-Chaykovsky oxirane generation through BF3-promoted 1,2-hydride shift yielding diphenylacetaldehyde.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Consider the following cascade starting from an unsymmetrical cyclic alkene:
$$\text{1-Methylcyclopent-1-ene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O_2,\ OH^-}]{\mathrm{(i)\ B_2H_6 / THF}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ PCC}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ CH_3MgBr}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D\ (major)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ CF_3CO_3H}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclopent-1-ene yields anti-Markovnikov alcohol A = trans-2-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.
2. (ii) PCC oxidation produces 2-methylcyclopentan-1-one (B).
3. (iii) Addition of CH3MgBr to ketone B yields tertiary alcohol C = 1,2-dimethylcyclopentan-1-ol.
4. (iv) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H2SO4 yields the tetrasubstituted Zaitsev alkene D = 1,2-dimethylcyclopent-1-ene.
5. (v) Epoxidation of D with trifluoroperacetic acid (CF3CO3H) forms tetrasubstituted bicyclic oxirane E = 1,2-dimethyl-6-oxabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Cyclic alkene hydroboration followed by oxidation, Grignard addition, Zaitsev dehydration, and peracid epoxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Hydroboration -> PCC oxidation -> Grignard addition -> Zaitsev elimination -> Epoxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Cyclic alkene regiocontrol, tertiary alcohol synthesis, Zaitsev tetrasubstituted alkene, oxirane synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Directs 1-methylcyclopentene through 5 steps to forge tetrasubstituted 1,2-dimethyl-6-oxabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane.

subject: Chemistry
question:
An aromatic ether cascade evaluates competitive ether cleavages:
$$\text{Phenol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{K_2CO_3,\ acetone}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Benzyl\ bromide}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{FeCl_3}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Cl_2\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{B\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ H_2,\ Pd/C}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{NaOH}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ CHCl_3\ (340\ K);\ then\ H^+}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ (CH_3CO)_2O,\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{C}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Benzylation of phenol with benzyl bromide and K2CO3 yields benzyl phenyl ether (A).
2. (ii) Monochlorination with Cl2/FeCl3: The bulky benzyloxy group (-OCH2Ph) directs electrophilic substitution predominantly to the unhindered para position, giving B = benzyl 4-chlorophenyl ether.
3. (iii) Catalytic hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C): Palladium selectively cleaves the benzylic C-O single bond via hydrogenolysis, liberating toluene and leaving the phenolic C-O bond intact to deliver C = 4-chlorophenol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Benzyl ether protection followed by para-chlorination and selective catalytic hydrogenolysis.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Benzylation -> Para-EAS chlorination -> Catalytic hydrogenolysis.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Benzyl protecting group, EAS regioselectivity, catalytic hydrogenolysis of benzyl ethers, phenol deprotection.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates selective cleavage of benzyl ether protecting groups over aryl-oxygen bonds.

subject: Chemistry
question:
In the following 5-step sequence involving a 1,2-diol:
$$\text{1,2-Diphenylethane-1,2-diol\ (Hydrobenzoin)} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(i)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ NaBH_4,\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ TsCl}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMF}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ t-BuOK,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ formed via Pinacol rearrangement is:
explanation:
1. (i) Pinacol rearrangement of hydrobenzoin, Ph-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-Ph: Protonation of one -OH followed by departure of water yields benzylic carbocation Ph-CH(+)-CH(OH)-Ph.
2. A 1,2-phenyl shift occurs to form the resonance-stabilized oxonium ion Ph2CH-CH=O+H, which deprotonates to give diphenylacetaldehyde, A = Ph2CH-CHO (rather than 1,2-diphenylethan-1-one).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Hydrobenzoin Pinacol rearrangement followed by reduction, tosylation, elimination, and epoxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Pinacol rearrangement -> Phenyl migratory shift -> Carbonyl formation.

subject: Chemistry
question:
An allylic alcohol is converted via tandem steps:
$$\text{But-3-en-2-ol} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ DMP}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_2=CH-MgBr}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ Grubbs\ catalyst\ (RCM)}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{(v)\ LiAlH_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{C}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) DMP oxidation of secondary allylic alcohol but-3-en-2-ol produces methyl vinyl ketone (A = but-3-en-2-one).
2. (ii) Addition of vinylmagnesium bromide to A gives tertiary bis-alkenyl alcohol B = 3-methylpenta-1,4-dien-3-ol.
3. (iii) Ring-Closing Metathesis (RCM) using Grubbs ruthenium catalyst couples the two terminal alkene groups with extrusion of volatile ethylene (CH2=CH2), closing a 4-membered cyclic allylic alcohol: C = 1-methylcyclobut-2-en-1-ol.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Allylic alcohol oxidation followed by vinyl Grignard addition and Grubbs ring-closing metathesis.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: DMP oxidation -> Vinyl Grignard addition -> Grubbs RCM cyclization.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Periodinane oxidation, divinyl carbinols, Grubbs olefin metathesis, cyclobutene synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Applies modern Grubbs ring-closing metathesis to forge strained 4-membered cyclic allylic alcohols.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A phenolic sequence explores regioselective carboxylations:
$$\text{o-Cresol (2-methylphenol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H^+} ]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaOH,\ CO_2\ (5\text{ atm},\ 410\text{ K})}} \mathbf{A\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_3OH,\ H_2SO_4,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{K_2CO_3}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ (CH_3)_2SO_4}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ excess\ CH_3MgBr}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ con.\ H_3PO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{A}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation of o-cresol (2-methylphenol) with NaOH and CO2 under pressure:
2. Coordination of the sodium cation (Na+) with the phenoxide oxygen directs the incoming CO2 electrophile specifically to the adjacent ortho position (chelation-controlled ortho substitution).
3. Since position 2 is occupied by the methyl group and position 1 is -OH, carboxylation occurs selectively at position 6 (the vacant ortho site), delivering A = 2-hydroxy-3-methylbenzoic acid (3-methylsalicylic acid).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation of ortho-cresol governed by sodium phenoxide chelation control.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Sodium phenoxide coordination -> Ortho-selective Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Cresol isomers, Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation, sodium chelation effect, substituted salicylic acids.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Enforces sodium chelation-controlled ortho-carboxylation in ortho-substituted phenols.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Ring contraction and ether functionalization is examined in:
$$\text{Cycloheptanol} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(i)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ NBS,\ DMSO,\ H_2O}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ NaH,\ THF}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3OH}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ PCC}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Acid-catalyzed dehydration of cycloheptanol yields cycloheptene (A).
2. (ii) Bromohydrin synthesis with NBS in aqueous DMSO yields trans-2-bromocycloheptan-1-ol (B).
3. (iii) Base-promoted intramolecular SN2 displacement by NaH closes the epoxide ring to form cycloheptene oxide (C = 8-oxabicyclo[5.1.0]octane).
4. (iv) Acid-catalyzed methanolysis opens the oxirane ring to give D = 2-methoxycycloheptan-1-ol.
5. (v) PCC oxidation of the secondary alcohol yields alpha-methoxy ketone E = 2-methoxycycloheptan-1-one.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: 7-membered cycloalkanol dehydration followed by halohydrin formation, epoxidation, ring opening, and PCC oxidation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Cycloalkene dehydration -> Bromohydrin -> Epoxide -> Methanolysis -> PCC oxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Medium ring cycloalkenes, oxirane synthesis in cycloheptyl systems, alpha-methoxy ketone preparation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Extends epoxide chemistry and selective functionalization to 7-membered cycloheptyl rings.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Trace the intermediates in the polyhydric phenol transformation:
$$\text{Catechol (benzene-1,2-diol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{K_2CO_3,\ DMF}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CH_2Br_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Br_2\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ THF}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ Mg}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Ethylene\ oxide}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ con.\ HI}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ contains which bicyclic heterocyclic system?
explanation:
1. (i) Reaction of catechol (benzene-1,2-diol) with dibromomethane (CH2Br2) in the presence of K2CO3 in DMF:
2. Both phenolic hydroxyl groups act as nucleophiles, undergoing sequential SN2 displacements on CH2Br2.
3. This closes a 5-membered methylenedioxy ring fused to the benzene core, forming A = 1,3-benzodioxole (benzo[d][1,3]dioxole).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Catechol bis-alkylation cyclization to 1,3-benzodioxole.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Double Williamson SN2 etherification -> 5-membered cyclic acetal/acetonide equivalent.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Catechol, methylenedioxy group, 1,3-benzodioxole synthesis, heterocyclic ethers.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Standardizes double nucleophilic displacement forming the natural product core 1,3-benzodioxole.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Competitive elimination vs. substitution of sterically hindered ethers:
$$\text{tert-Butyl alcohol} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(i)\ NaH,\ THF}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ 1-bromobutane}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ HBr\ (con.),\ \Delta}} \mathbf{C\ (alkyl\ halide)} + \mathbf{D} \quad \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ alc.\ KOH,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{E} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ O_3;\ then\ Zn/H_2O}} \mathbf{F}$$
If $\mathbf{C}$ is the alkyl bromide originating from the butyl chain, compound $\mathbf{F}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Sodium tert-butoxide (A) attacks primary 1-bromobutane via SN2 to yield tert-butyl butyl ether (B).
2. (iii) Cleavage with excess hot concentrated HBr: The tert-butyl group is cleaved via SN1 (giving tert-butyl bromide or isobutylene), while the primary butyl group is cleaved via SN2 attack of bromide, giving C = 1-bromobutane.
3. (iv) Dehydrohalogenation of 1-bromobutane with alcoholic KOH gives terminal alkene E = but-1-ene (CH3CH2CH=CH2).
4. (v) Reductive ozonolysis (O3 then Zn/H2O) of but-1-ene cleaves the double bond to yield F = propanal (CH3CH2CHO) and formaldehyde (HCHO).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Williamson ether synthesis followed by acidic ether cleavage, E2 elimination, and reductive ozonolysis.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Williamson synthesis -> HBr ether cleavage -> E2 dehydrohalogenation -> Ozonolytic cleavage.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Asymmetric ether synthesis, dual SN1/SN2 ether cleavage mechanisms, Hofmann/Zaitsev elimination, alkene ozonolysis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Connects selective cleavage of asymmetric alkyl ethers with terminal alkene ozonolysis.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A Grignard-driven ether synthesis cascade proceeds as follows:
$$\text{2-Bromopropane} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{ether}]{\mathrm{(i)\ Mg}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Propylene\ oxide}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ DMP}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ CH_3Li}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ Cu\ at\ 573\text{ K}}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i)-(ii) Isopropylmagnesium bromide attacks propylene oxide (2-methyloxirane) at the less sterically hindered primary carbon (C1) followed by protonation, giving secondary alcohol B = 4-methylpentan-2-ol.
2. (iii) DMP oxidizes B to ketone C = 4-methylpentan-2-one.
3. (iv) Methyllithium (CH3Li) adds to ketone C to produce tertiary alcohol D = 2,4-dimethylpentan-2-ol.
4. (v) Hot copper at 573 K: Tertiary alcohols do not possess an alpha-hydrogen and cannot undergo dehydrogenation to carbonyls; instead, they undergo facile catalytic dehydration to yield the most substituted Zaitsev alkene: E = 2,4-dimethylpent-2-ene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Epoxide Grignard ring opening followed by oxidation, organolithium addition, and Cu-catalyzed tertiary alcohol dehydration.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Steric-controlled oxirane opening -> DMP oxidation -> Organolithium addition -> Cu/573 K dehydration.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Oxirane ring opening regiochemistry, tertiary alcohol synthesis, catalytic copper behavior on 3° alcohols.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Distinguishes copper catalytic dehydrogenation (1°/2° alcohols) from copper-induced dehydration (3° alcohols).

subject: Chemistry
question:
The following reaction pathway exploits the Dow's process and subsequent substitutions:
$$\text{Chlorobenzene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{623\ K,\ 300\text{ atm}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ aq.\ NaOH;\ then\ H^+}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Br_2\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{B\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ CH_3I,\ K_2CO_3}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ CO_2;\ (3)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Mg,\ ether}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ con.\ HI}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Dow's process: Severe conditions (623 K, 300 atm) with aqueous NaOH followed by acidification hydrolyze chlorobenzene to phenol (A) via a benzyne/addition-elimination mechanism.
2. (ii) Bromination in acetic acid yields 4-bromophenol (B) as the major para product.
3. (iii) Methylation gives 4-bromoanisole (C).
4. (iv) Grignard formation followed by carboxylation with CO2 and acidic quench gives D = 4-methoxybenzoic acid (p-anisic acid).
5. (v) Demethylation with excess hot concentrated HI cleaves the aryl methyl ether bond without affecting the benzoic acid group, delivering E = 4-hydroxybenzoic acid.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Industrial Dow's process coupled with para-bromination, etherification, Grignard carboxylation, and HI demethylation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Dow's process -> Para-bromination -> Williamson synthesis -> Grignard carboxylation -> HI demethylation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Aromatic nucleophilic substitution, phenol bromination, Grignard carbonation, selective aryl ether cleavage.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Unifies industrial phenol synthesis with Grignard carboxylation and chemoselective ether cleavage.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Epoxide ring cleavage with carbon nucleophiles:
$$\text{Cyclopentene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ NaC\equiv CH}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ HgSO_4,\ H_2O}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{NaOH}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ I_2\ (excess)}} \mathbf{D} + \ce{CHI3}\downarrow \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Epoxidation of cyclopentene with mCPBA gives cyclopentene oxide (A).
2. (ii) Sodium acetylide attacks the oxirane ring with inversion to give B = trans-2-ethynylcyclopentan-1-ol.
3. (iii) Kucherov hydration (HgSO4/H2SO4) of the terminal alkyne converts it into a methyl ketone: C = 1-(2-hydroxycyclopentyl)ethan-1-one.
4. (iv)-(v) Haloform reaction with excess I2/NaOH oxidizes the methyl ketone to a carboxylate with yellow CHI3 precipitate. Acidification yields E = 2-hydroxycyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Oxirane ring opening with sodium acetylide followed by alkyne hydration and haloform carboxylic acid generation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Epoxidation -> Acetylide SN2 opening -> Kucherov hydration -> Haloform oxidation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Oxirane cleavage by alkynyl carbanions, alkyne hydration to methyl ketones, haloform cleavage.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates alkynyl carbanion opening of epoxides followed by Kucherov-haloform degradation.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Vicinal diol cleavage and intramolecular aldol:
$$\text{Cyclohept-1-ene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)\ OsO_4,\ NaIO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(ii)\ dil.\ aq.\ NaOH}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ NaBH_4,\ CH_3OH}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{(v)\ LiAlH_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Lemieux-Johnson oxidative cleavage (OsO4/NaIO4) cleaves the double bond of cycloheptene to give 1,7-heptanedial (A = OHC-(CH2)5-CHO).
2. (ii) Intramolecular aldol condensation: Under dilute basic conditions, enolization occurs at C2/C6. Attack of the enolate on the second carbonyl closes a stable 5-membered ring (rather than a strained 7-membered ring). Dehydration yields the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde: B = cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Cycloheptene oxidative ring opening followed by intramolecular aldol condensation to a cyclopentenyl enal.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Lemieux-Johnson cleavage -> Intramolecular aldol condensation -> Enal dehydration.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Alkene oxidative cleavage, dialdehyde cyclization, 5-membered ring thermodynamic preference in aldol.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Directs heptanedial selectively into cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde via aldol ring-closure.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Examine the ether cascade involving chiral oxiranes:
$$\text{(R)-2-methyloxirane} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3OH}]{\mathrm{(i)\ cat.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{py}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ TsCl}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ NaBr,\ DMF}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ ether}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Mg}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(v)\ HCHO}} \mathbf{E}$$
Step (i) proceeds with nucleophilic attack primarily at which carbon, and with what stereochemical outcome?
options: At C2 (more substituted) with complete retention of configuration
At C2 (more substituted) with predominant inversion of configuration
At C3 (less substituted) via pure SN2 retention
At C3 (less substituted) via radical pathway
explanation:
1. Under acidic conditions, the oxirane oxygen of (R)-2-methyloxirane is protonated.
2. The bond to the more substituted secondary carbon (C2) lengthens significantly, developing substantial carbocation character.
3. The weak nucleophile methanol (CH3OH) attacks predominantly at the more substituted C2 position.
4. Because the nucleophile attacks from the backside opposite to the breaking C-O bond, the reaction proceeds with predominant INVERSION of configuration at C2.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Stereochemical and regiochemical analysis of chiral oxirane acidic methanolysis.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Acid-promoted epoxide opening -> Attack at more substituted center -> Inversion of stereochemistry.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Chiral epoxides, acidic ring opening, carbocation character vs steric control, Walden inversion.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Tests crucial stereochemical inversion at the more substituted carbon during acidic epoxide methanolysis.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Multi-step synthesis involving phenolic azo-coupling:
$$\text{Aniline} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{273-278\text{ K}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaNO_2,\ HCl}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{pH\ 9-10}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Phenol}} \mathbf{B\ (orange\ dye)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ (CH_3)_2SO_4,\ NaOH}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ SnCl_2}} \mathbf{D} + \text{Aniline} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ Br_2}} \mathbf{E}$$
Compound $\mathbf{D}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Diazotization of aniline gives benzenediazonium chloride (A).
2. (ii) Azo coupling with phenol in alkaline medium (pH 9-10) couples at the para position to form orange dye B = 4-(phenyldiazenyl)phenol (p-hydroxyazobenzene).
3. (iii) Methylation of the phenolic -OH with dimethyl sulfate gives C = 1-methoxy-4-(phenyldiazenyl)benzene.
4. (iv) Reductive cleavage of the azo double bond (-N=N-) with SnCl2/HCl cleaves the molecule into two primary aromatic amines: aniline and D = 4-methoxyaniline (p-anisidine).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Diazotization followed by phenolic azo-coupling, etherification, and reductive azo cleavage.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Diazotization -> Phenol azo coupling -> Phenolic methylation -> Reductive azo cleavage.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Azo coupling pH control, phenoxide etherification, SnCl2 azo reduction, p-anisidine synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Unpacks azo coupling and subsequent reductive cleavage to access para-substituted anisidine derivatives.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Pinacol rearrangement involving unsymmetrical aryl systems:
$$\text{1,1-diphenyl-2-methylpropane-1,2-diol} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(i)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{A\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ NaBH_4}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ con.\ H_3PO_4}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O_2,\ OH^-}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ B_2H_6 / THF}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(v)\ PCC}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ formed via migratory aptitude preference is:
explanation:
1. In 1,1-diphenyl-2-methylpropane-1,2-diol, protonation occurs preferentially at the carbon bearing the two phenyl groups (C1) because departure of water generates an exceptionally stable resonance-stabilized benzhydryl carbocation: Ph2C(+)-C(OH)(CH3)2.
2. Between the two methyl groups at C2, a 1,2-methyl shift takes place onto the benzhydryl carbocation with concomitant formation of the C=O double bond.
3. This delivers ketone A = 3,3-diphenylbutan-2-one.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Pinacol rearrangement of an unsymmetrical benzhydryl diol governed by carbocation stability and methyl shift.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Selective benzylic carbocation formation -> 1,2-methyl shift -> Carbonyl formation.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Pinacol rearrangement, carbocation stability (benzhydryl vs aliphatic 3°), migratory aptitude.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates that initial carbocation stability overrides normal aryl-migratory aptitude.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Functional manipulation of allylic phenoxy systems:
$$\text{2-Allylphenol} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(i)\ cat.\ TsOH,\ benzene}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CCl_4}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ NBS,\ h\nu}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{DMSO}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ t-BuOK,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{(v)\ LiAlH_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Heating 2-allylphenol with catalytic TsOH in benzene protonates the terminal double bond to generate a secondary carbocation on the propyl chain.
2. The internal phenolic -OH group performs an intramolecular nucleophilic attack on this secondary carbocation.
3. Cyclization closes a 5-membered cyclic ether (5-exo-trig process), delivering A = 2-methyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Acid-catalyzed intramolecular oxa-addition of 2-allylphenol to 2-methyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Alkene protonation -> Intramolecular phenolic addition -> 5-exo-trig dihydrofuran closure.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: 2-allylphenol cyclization, Markovnikov protonation, Baldwin rules in ether cyclization.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Reinforces 5-exo-trig closure producing 2-methyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran rather than 6-membered chroman.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Selective oxidation and coupling in aromatic ether sequences:
$$\text{Anisole} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CH_3OCH_2Cl,\ TiCl_4}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{acetone}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ NaI}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ ether}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ Mg}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Acetone}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{E}$$
The major organic product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Chloromethylation (Blanc-type) of anisole occurs predominantly at the para position to form A = 1-(chloromethyl)-4-methoxybenzene (4-methoxybenzyl chloride).
2. (ii) Finkelstein exchange with NaI yields 4-methoxybenzyl iodide (B).
3. (iii) Reaction with magnesium in dry ether forms benzylic Grignard reagent C = (4-methoxybenzyl)magnesium iodide.
4. (iv) Nucleophilic addition of Grignard C to acetone followed by protonation yields tertiary alcohol D = 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)-2-methylpropan-2-ol.
5. (v) Acid-catalyzed dehydration with hot H2SO4 yields the conjugated alkene: E = 1-methoxy-4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl)benzene.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Anisole chloromethylation followed by Finkelstein exchange, Grignard formation, addition, and conjugated dehydration.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Chloromethylation -> Finkelstein exchange -> Grignard addition -> Conjugated dehydration.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Aromatic chloromethylation, benzylic Grignards, ketone additions, conjugated styrene derivative synthesis.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Constructs a conjugated alkoxy-stilbene-like system via benzylic Grignard addition and dehydration.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Ether peroxide degradation and alcohol identification:
$$\text{Diethyl ether} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{h\nu}]{\mathrm{(i)\ O_2\ (air,\ prolonged)}} \mathbf{A\ (peroxide)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ FeSO_4\ (test)}} \text{Color change} \quad \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iii)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ excess\ I_2,\ NaOH}} \mathbf{D}\downarrow + \mathbf{E} \quad \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ Ag\ powder}} \mathbf{F}$$
Precipitate $\mathbf{D}$ and terminal hydrocarbon $\mathbf{F}$ are:
explanation:
1. (i) Autoxidation of diethyl ether upon prolonged exposure to air/light forms 1-ethoxyethyl hydroperoxide (A).
2. (ii) FeSO4 test detects peroxides through oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ (forming blood-red Fe(SCN)3 with KCNS).
3. (iii) Acidic hydrolysis of peroxide A cleaves the peroxy ether into ethanol and acetaldehyde (B = CH3CHO).
4. (iv) Acetaldehyde (having a CH3-C=O group) undergoes the iodoform reaction with I2/NaOH to form yellow precipitate D = triiodomethane (CHI3).
5. (v) Heating iodoform with finely divided silver powder abstracts iodine to yield acetylene: F = ethyne (CH#CH).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Ether autoxidation peroxide formation cascaded with hydrolysis, iodoform reaction, and silver powder reduction to acetylene.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Ether autoxidation -> Hydrolysis to acetaldehyde -> Iodoform reaction -> Dehalogenative coupling to acetylene.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Ether peroxide hazard and detection, haloform test, iodoform reduction by silver to acetylene.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Connects practical ether peroxide hazards with iodoform precipitation and acetylene generation.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Epoxide rearrangement in terpene precursors:
$$\text{1-Methylcyclohexene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(i)\ mCPBA}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{ether}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ BF_3\cdot OEt_2}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ C_6H_5MgBr}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ Me_2S}]{\mathrm{(v)\ (1)\ O_3}} \mathbf{E}$$
Rearrangement product $\mathbf{B}$ formed via Lewis-acid coordination is:
explanation:
1. (i) Epoxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene with mCPBA forms 1-methylcyclohexene oxide (A).
2. (ii) Coordination of Lewis acid BF3.OEt2 to the epoxide oxygen triggers selective opening of the C-O bond at the tertiary carbon, developing tertiary carbocation character.
3. To relieve ring strain and achieve rapid stabilization, the C1-C6 ring bond undergoes a 1,2-shift (ring contraction), forging a cyclopentane ring and delivering ketone B = cyclopentyl methyl ketone (c-C5H9-COCH3).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: 1-Methylcyclohexene epoxidation followed by BF3-promoted carbocyclic ring contraction.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Epoxidation -> Lewis acid complexation -> 1,2-bond migration ring contraction.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Epoxide Lewis acid rearrangements, ring contraction, methyl ketone generation.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Pinpoints the selective ring contraction of 1-methylcyclohexene oxide to cyclopentyl methyl ketone.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Synthesis involving the Kolbe--Schmitt carboxylate cascade:
$$\text{Resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H^+}]{\mathrm{(i)\ KHCO_3,\ CO_2,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ excess\ (CH_3)_2SO_4,\ NaOH}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ LiAlH_4,\ then\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ PCC}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ con.\ HI}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{A}$ formed via carboxylation between the two activating groups is:
explanation:
1. (i) In resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol), both hydroxyl groups exert cooperative ortho/para activating effects on position 2 (which is ortho to both -OH groups).
2. Carboxylation using potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) and CO2 under heating selectively introduces the carboxyl group at this mutually activated position 2, delivering A = 2,6-dihydroxybenzoic acid (gamma-resorcylic acid).

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Resorcinol regioselective carboxylation followed by methylation, reduction, oxidation, and demethylation.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Cooperative EAS carboxylation -> Permethylation -> Ester/acid reduction -> PCC oxidation -> HI cleavage.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Resorcinol cooperative directing effects, Kolbe-Schmitt modifications, resorcylic acid isomers.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Demonstrates selective carboxylation at C2 yielding 2,6-dihydroxybenzoic acid.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Victor Meyer test and nitroalkane reductions:
$$\text{Propan-2-ol} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(i)\ P/I_2}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ AgNO_2}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iii)\ HNO_2}} \mathbf{C\ (blue)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{(iv)\ Sn}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CHCl_3}]{\mathrm{(v)\ alc.\ KOH,\ \Delta}} \mathbf{E}$$
Intermediate $\mathbf{C}$ is known as:
explanation:
1. (i) Propan-2-ol (secondary alcohol) reacts with P/I2 to form 2-iodopropane (A).
2. (ii) Nucleophilic substitution with AgNO2 yields secondary nitroalkane B = 2-nitropropane, (CH3)2CH-NO2.
3. (iii) Reaction with nitrous acid (HNO2): 2-Nitropropane has one alpha-hydrogen and reacts with HNO2 to form 2-nitro-2-nitrosopropane (C), commonly called pseudonitrol.
4. Pseudonitrol is intensely blue in organic solvents and unreactive toward alkali, providing the diagnostic blue color test for secondary alcohols in Victor Meyer's procedure.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Secondary alcohol Victor Meyer progression evaluated through pseudonitrol formation and carbylamine reaction.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Victor Meyer sequence -> Secondary nitroalkane -> Pseudonitrol -> Reduction -> Carbylamine test.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Victor Meyer test, secondary alcohol identification, pseudonitrol chemistry, carbylamine reaction.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Pinpoints the exact identity and characteristic blue chromophore of 2-nitro-2-nitrosopropane.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Steric outcome in unsymmetrical ether cleavage:
$$\text{2-Methoxy-2-phenylpropane} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{anhydrous}]{\mathrm{(i)\ 1\ eq.\ HBr\ (0^\circ\text{C})}} \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B\ (volatile)} \quad \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{dry\ ether}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ Mg}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ CO_2}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ SOCl_2}} \mathbf{E} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{(v)\ Benzene}} \mathbf{F}$$
Halide $\mathbf{A}$ and alcohol $\mathbf{B}$ are formed by which mechanistic pathway?
explanation:
1. 2-Methoxy-2-phenylpropane contains a tertiary benzylic carbon.
2. In the presence of anhydrous HBr at 0°C, the ether oxygen is protonated to form an oxonium ion.
3. Because the cumyl carbocation, Ph-C+(CH3)2, is exceptionally stable (both tertiary and benzylically resonance-stabilized), C-O bond cleavage proceeds via an SN1 pathway.
4. Methanol departs as neutral leaving group B (volatile), and bromide rapidly traps the stable carbocation to give A = 2-bromo-2-phenylpropane.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Ether cleavage mechanistic differentiation (SN1 vs SN2) on a tertiary benzylic ether.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Protonation -> Heterolytic C-O cleavage -> SN1 carbocation capture.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Ether cleavage by HX, SN1 vs SN2 criteria, benzylic tertiary carbocation stability.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Enforces SN1 mechanistic pathway yielding 2-bromo-2-phenylpropane and methanol.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Fries rearrangement and subsequent cleavages:
$$\text{Phenyl acetate} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2,\ 298\text{ K}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ anhydrous\ AlCl_3}} \mathbf{A\ (para\ major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(ii)\ CH_3CH_2I,\ K_2CO_3}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{NaOH}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ excess\ Br_2}} \mathbf{C} + \ce{CHBr3}\downarrow \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(iv)\ H_3O^+}} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(v)\ excess\ con.\ HI}} \mathbf{E}$$
Product $\mathbf{E}$ is:
explanation:
1. (i) Fries rearrangement of phenyl acetate at low temperature (298 K in CS2) favors the thermodynamically stable para isomer: A = 4-hydroxyacetophenone.
2. (ii) Ethylation with ethyl iodide and K2CO3 converts the phenol into an ethyl ether, giving B = 4-ethoxyacetophenone.
3. (iii)-(iv) Haloform reaction: Excess Br2/NaOH oxidizes the methyl ketone to a carboxylate with precipitation of bromoform (CHBr3). Acidification yields D = 4-ethoxybenzoic acid.
4. (v) Ether cleavage with excess hot concentrated HI hydrolyzes the ethyl ether (-OCH2CH3 -> -OH + CH3CH2I) while leaving the benzoic acid intact, delivering E = 4-hydroxybenzoic acid.

originalityAudit.problemStructure: Phenyl acetate Fries rearrangement followed by ethylation, haloform oxidation, and selective HI ether cleavage.
originalityAudit.solutionMethodSignature: Para-Fries rearrangement -> Etherification -> Haloform cleavage -> Acidic ether deprotection.
originalityAudit.conceptCombination: Fries rearrangement temperature control, haloform degradation, selective ether cleavage.
originalityAudit.noveltyRationale: Combines low-temperature para-selective Fries rearrangement with haloform oxidation and ether cleavage.

subject: Chemistry
question:
A ring-opening cascade of oxetanes (4-membered cyclic ethers):
$$\text{Oxetane (trimethylene oxide)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(i)\ C_6H_5MgBr\ (1\ eq.)}} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}]{\mathrm{(ii)\ PCC}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(2)\ H_3O^+}]{\mathrm{(iii)\ CH_3MgBr}} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{(iv)\ con.\ H_2SO_4}} \mathbf{D\ (major)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{(v)\ B_2H_6;\ then\ H_2O_2,\ OH^-}} \mathbf{E}$$
